extracted.intended_audience: American travelers and general readers interested in Paris (mid-19th century)
extracted.subtask_description: First-person travel-essay reporting on Parisian social life, institutions (opera, ballet, museums), politics, and public administration, written for American readers considering or curious about Europe. Contains evaluative judgments and prescriptive comments about culture, art, and civic practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opera-house physical and managerial qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The house is very spacious, admirably planned, superbly fitted up; the charges moderate; the audience large and well dressed; the officers and attendants up to their business, and everything orderly and quiet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a national institution the Opera should offer ample space and good planning, decent fittings, reasonable prices, decorous audiences, competent staff, and orderly performances. These features mark an Opera fit for broad social attendance and public support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative importance of spectacle versus music in opera
rubrics_metrics.description: This is a drama of Action and of Spectacle, however, to which the Music is subordinate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate an opera by whether its dramatic spectacle dominates and the music serves it; presence of grand stage action and large casts indicates spectacle-oriented works even if musical quality is unremarkable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting and vocal excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: There were no great singers included in the cast for this evening... I am a poor judge, but I should say the music is not remarkable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess productions by presence of leading singers: absence of 'great singers' is grounds to judge the musical aspect as weak despite spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness and moral effect of ballet and stage dancing
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Opera is ever to become an element of Social life... such a one as thoughtful men may take their daughters to witness without apprehension or remorse. I do not know whether the Opera we now have is or is not such a one; I know _this_ is not. Its entire, palpable, urgent tendency, is 'earthly, sensual, devilish.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge ballets and stage dances for their effect on public morals: they should strengthen purity and be suitable for family attendance. Warning signs include overt sexual display, excessive sensuality, or an institutional tendency to weaken moral instincts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable style of dance (grace vs grotesque feats)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'poetry of motion,' of harmonious evolutions and the graceful movement of 'twinkling feet'... But what grace, what sense, what witchery, there can be, for instance, in a young girl's standing on one great toe and raising the other foot to the altitude of her head... As an exhibition of muscular power, it is disagreeable to me... Why is it kept on the stage?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer dance that emphasizes grace, harmonious movement, health, and modesty. Treat extreme acrobatic contortions and feats obtained by severe and protracted suffering as disagreeable and potentially exploitative; applause by hired 'claqueurs' for such feats is an anti-pattern indicating vulgarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicator of vulgarity: claqueurs' applause
rubrics_metrics.description: nearly all the applause bestowed on those ballet-feats ... came from the little knot of hired 'claqueurs' in the center of the pit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat disproportionate applause coming from a visible hired group as an indicator that a performance element panders to vulgar tastes rather than genuine aesthetic appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibition and jury-based adjudication principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of the Exhibition is not merely to set forth what is best but to compare it with the inferior, and so indicate the readiest mode of improving the latter... I appeal with confidence to the awards of the various Juries appointed by the Royal Commissioners. They are competent; they have made the requisite examinations; they (though nearly all European and a majority of them British) are honorable men, and will render an impartial judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhibitions should include both superior and inferior examples to permit comparison and improvement. Final assessment should rest with competent, impartial juries who perform requisite examinations rather than with premature press censure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about press impartiality in industry criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: The self-constituted arbiters who thus tell the American people that Art is not their province... are they impartial advisers? Are they not palpably speaking in the interest of the rival producers of Europe?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating criticism of national industry, account for potential bias from press or commentators with commercial interests; press disparagement can be motivated by protectionism rather than honest assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and moral responsibility of public art collections
rubrics_metrics.description: The Battles ... are here as imposing as paint can make them, but never a whisper of Agincourt, Crecy, Poictiers, Blenheim, or Ramillies... The whole collection is, in its general effect, delusive and mischievous, the purpose being to exhibit War as always glorious and France as uniformly triumphant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate public battle paintings and memorial art not only for artistic merit but for truthfulness and moral effect; collections that suppress defeats and exclusively glorify war are misleading and morally harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for repurposing royal palaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of them may be converted into Hospitals, Insane Retreats, &c., others into Libraries or Galleries of Art and Science... Perhaps it will be best... to convert all the others into direct uses and preserve this (Versailles) for public inspection as a perpetual memorial of the reckless prodigality...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When large former royal residences become publicly owned, prefer conversions that serve direct public needs (hospitals, retreats, libraries, galleries) or use some as public memorials illustrating past profligacy; consider proximity to population centers and cost-effectiveness in deciding uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public spending and architectural proportion critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly all the public buildings of Paris strike me as lacking height in proportion to their superficial dimensions... Versailles alone cost some Thirty Millions of Dollars at first... France has paid more as simple interest on the residences of her monarchs... than the United States... pays for the entire cost of the Legislative, Executive and Judicial departments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess monumental public expenditure by comparing architectural effect (proportion and utility) with social cost; lavish royal building that burdens the populace is subject to moral and civic criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passport enforcement and traveler burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man who lodges a stranger here must see forthwith that he has a Passport in good condition, in default of which said host is liable to a penalty... It has cost me precious hours already, not to speak of dollars... It is a shame that Republican France stands far behind Aristocratic Britain in this respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat strict passport checks and attendant bureaucracy as a significant impediment to travel; hosts are required to verify passports, and opaque or humorous profession entries (e.g., 'Loafer', 'Rowdy') can cause perplexity, highlighting poor implementation of passport rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher-law moral standard for soldiers and officials
rubrics_metrics.description: No one has a moral right to do as a soldier that which it would be wrong for him to do as a man... every man owes a paramount obedience to the law of God, and cannot excuse his violation of that law by producing an order to do so from any functionary or potentate whatever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating military or official conduct, apply the principle that obedience to orders does not excuse acts morally wrong; individuals bear moral responsibility and higher-law obligations above mere legal commands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of imminent peril to republican government
rubrics_metrics.description: The immediate peril of the Republic is the Election of May, '52, in view of the arbitrary disfranchisement of nearly one-half the Democratic voters, the manacled condition of the Press, the denial to the People of the Right of Meeting for deliberation and concert, and the betrayal of all the enormous power and patronage of the State into the hands of the Aristocratic party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess threats to a republic by checking for systematic disenfranchisement, press suppression, denial of assembly rights, and concentration of state patronage in an anti-democratic faction; these are warning metrics of democratic backsliding.
